A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to fever, malaise, and nausea for the past week.  The patient has no significant medical history but regularly uses intravenous recreational drugs.  Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F).  On physical examination, there is scleral icterus.  A tender, smooth liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin.  He is managed with supportive care and undergoes serial serologic testing during outpatient follow-up.  The following graph illustrates this patient's hepatitis B serologic markers over time.

Which of the following best explains the changes in this patient's serologic markers over the period shown?​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​

explanation:
Importance of hepatitis B serologic markers

HBsAg

  • HBV surface glycoproteins
  • First serologic marker of acute infection
  • Persistence >6 months = chronic infection

HBeAg

  • HBV polypeptide
  • Detectable in acute infection & may persist in chronic infection
  • Indicates ↑ viral replication & infectivity

Anti-HBc IgM

  • First antibody in acute infection
  • May be only marker of recent infection during window period (after HBsAg clearance, before anti-HBs)

Anti-HBs

  • Seen with cleared infection or vaccination
  • Confers long-term immunity

Anti-HBe

  • Develops in cleared infection & later in chronic infection
  • Indicates ↓ viral replication & infectivity

Anti-HBc IgG

  • Appears during acute infection & persists for life (resolved or chronic)
  • Not present after vaccination

Serologic markers for hepatitis B virus (HBV) can be used to distinguish between acute infection, chronic infection, resolved infection, and a protective vaccination response.  Acute infection is marked by replication of the virus in hepatocytes with the release of viral antigens (HBsAg, HBeAg) and HBV DNA into the bloodstream.  HBsAg is the first serologic marker to appear, followed shortly by IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), the first antibody to be detected.  Most adults with acute infection have subclinical, anicteric disease, but approximately 30% develop jaundice, malaise, and tender hepatomegaly lasting weeks to months.

Approximately 95% of immunocompetent adults with acute HBV infection clear HBsAg and generate protective immunity against future infection.  Resolution is reflected serologically by the following progression:

  1. HBeAg disappears and anti-HBe antibodies develop, generally indicating reduced viral replication and infectivity.

  2. HBsAg is cleared shortly afterward, typically by 4-6 months after infection.

  3. Anti-HBs antibodies appear weeks to months after HBsAg is cleared and provide protective immunity against future infection.

  4. IgM anti-HBc wanes over the following months, whereas IgG anti-HBc persists for life as a marker of past infection.

The interval between HBsAg clearance and anti-HBs detection is the window period.  Anti-HBe and IgG anti-HBc are usually also present, but because both persist long after infection, IgM anti-HBc may be the only marker of recent infection.

This patient's graph shows resolution of infection.  At the time of the emergency department visit, HBsAg, HBeAg, and IgM anti-HBc are elevated, indicating acute hepatitis B with high infectivity.  HBeAg and HBsAg are cleared by ~4 months, and anti-HBs appears after a brief window period.  By 10 months, IgG anti-HBc and anti-HBs are present without viral antigens, indicating recovery with immunity against reinfection.

(Choices A and B)  Chronic hepatitis B is defined by persistence of HBsAg for >6 months.  High infectivity is marked by HBeAg and high HBV DNA levels without anti-HBe.  Transition to low infectivity usually occurs years later and is marked by HBeAg clearance, development of anti-HBe, and lower HBV DNA levels (along with continued HBsAg production).  Although this patient was HBeAg positive (ie, highly infectious) at presentation, he cleared both HBeAg and HBsAg by ~4 months, which excludes chronic infection.

(Choice C)  Patients with an exacerbation of chronic hepatitis B have an abrupt increase in liver enzymes and increased levels of HBV DNA.  Exacerbations are often asymptomatic, but some individuals develop symptoms of acute hepatitis.  However, these patients typically remain HBsAg positive and do not develop anti-HBs antibodies.

(Choice D)  Vaccination against hepatitis B would be identified by the presence of anti-HBs with no anti-HBc, anti-HBe, or viral antigens because the recombinant vaccine contains only HBsAg.  This patient's anti-HBc indicates natural infection.

Educational objective:The presence of IgG anti-HBc and anti-HBs antibodies in the serum without detectable viral antigens indicates recovery from acute hepatitis B infection with immunity against reinfection.  In contrast, patients vaccinated against hepatitis B will have anti-HBs antibodies without detectable levels of anti-HBc.  Chronic hepatitis B is indicated by persistence of HBsAg in the serum for >6 months.​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​
